summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Quindío is Colombia's national one, and it is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to premises and to detention is governed by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence, and the source inventory records no Quindío-specific incident, enforcement action or legal restriction. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died that afternoon. Police questioned local residents, but no one was arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was."

Nationally, 13 trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023. Earlier national incidents cited include killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed actors. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyers delivered on the street and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets and announced a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; three armed men gave a trans woman and local election candidate one week to leave town, she hid for a week and then fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend had been killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024. Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and discrimination leaves trans women in the department mainly with hairdressing or sex work.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
The violence documented in the inventory is concentrated in departments under armed-group control and is tied to Colombia's decades-long civil conflict rather than to any Quindío-specific dispute. Guajira and Caquetá are named as the locations of kill-list and "social cleansing" flyer campaigns; the Millerey killing occurred in Bello, Antioquia. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case and are described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the conflict.

Displacement by armed actors is an adjacent risk: in Caquetá a trans woman election candidate was given one week to leave town and fled at night, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. The same reporting counts eight trans women killed nationally between February and April 2024, 41 in 2023, 13 in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders recorded by the Attorney General's Office between January and May 2025.

The gap between statute and practice is the main comparative point: the UN Independent Expert Graeme Reid praised Colombia's legal reforms in May 2025 while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Quindío-specific legal, enforcement, facilities or incident finding. The EL PAÍS report of 14 April 2025 and The Guardian report of 30 July 2024 both make that absence explicit: their bearing on Quindío is national context and the pattern of territorial violence by armed actors in other departments. Whether Quindío's own police, notaries or premises have trans-related enforcement records is not sourced here.

The account of Sara Millerey's death is inconsistent across sources: the parent framework describes her flailing in a creek outside Medellín, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before drowning, while EL PAÍS reports an attack on 4 April 2025 and death from cardiac arrest that afternoon. The date of the assault (4 April), the viral video (5 April) and the absence of an arrest are common to both. The discrepancy is unresolved.

Two counts of the same national figure appear in different wording: more than 40 transgender women killed in 2023, and 41 in 2023. Both are reproduced above as given; no reconciliation of the underlying data is available in the inventory.
